title: I am who am (Exodus 3:14)
hook: the name God gives Moses at the burning bush

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Magisterium: a teaching office that serves the word, not above it. Your line was servants of the word. Now, what does the word say about God himself?

A shepherd on a mountain in the desert. A bush is on fire and doesn't burn up. A voice from it tells him to go back to Egypt, face Pharaoh, and lead a nation of slaves to freedom. And he asks the most reasonable question there is: who should I say sent me? What's your name? A name tells you who someone is, or at least how to call them. The answer Moses gets is hardly a name at all. Today: Aquinas.
screen: `A BUSH THAT DOESN'T BURN UP.` → `WHO SHOULD I SAY SENT ME?` → `HARDLY A NAME AT ALL.`

segments.voice: First, the answer. In the Douay-Rheims, God says to Moses: "I AM WHO AM." And then: tell the people of Israel, "HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you." In Hebrew it's three words, ehyeh asher ehyeh, built on the verb to be. Scholars still debate how to translate it: I am who I am, or I will be who I will be. Jews read and treasure this passage too, and traditionally don't pronounce the holy four-letter name God gives in the next verse. Second, a name that won't be pinned down. This is a name that refuses to be a handle. The Catechism says it's both revealed and mysterious: God tells Moses who he is, and at the same time stays beyond grasping. Third, being itself. Thomas Aquinas called HE WHO IS the most fitting name for God. For him, God doesn't just have existence, the way a tree or a star has it. God is existence. Everything else has its being on loan; God simply is. Remember young Merton on the train, nearly throwing out a philosophy book? This was the idea that stopped him. The Catechism calls God the fullness of being. Fourth, the Gospel echo. In John's Gospel, Jesus says: "Amen, amen I say to you, before Abraham was made, I AM." Christians hear in those words a claim to the name from the bush. Catholics take that to mean the God who simply is came close enough to be spoken to by name.
screen: `EHYEH ASHER EHYEH.` · `A NAME THAT ISN'T A HANDLE.` · `NOT A BEING, BUT BEING ITSELF.` · `BEFORE ABRAHAM WAS MADE, I AM.` · then, large: `I AM WHO AM.`

segments.voice: On each out-breath, say quietly, inside: I am. Not I am busy, or tired, or behind; just I am, and notice that you simply exist, right now, without doing anything to earn it. Catholics believe every moment of that existence is borrowed from God, who simply is; if you pray, you can rest there, held in being.
Aquinas, the theologian who called God's name at the bush, HE WHO IS, the most fitting name, because God simply is existence. Today's word.
Your line: being itself. No achievement needed, just: I am. Day two hundred ninety-five.

howItsDone: Catholics hear the burning bush read at Mass, and out of reverence the Church asks that the Hebrew divine name not be spoken aloud in the liturgy, where it is rendered as the Lord.

notes: Editor review 2026-10-01: cut the sweeping "every other god in the ancient world had a name ... bargained with" (unfair to other ancient religions and uncited); "the strangest name in the Bible" and "the most powerful man in the world" superlatives removed; the unpronounced holy name is now placed correctly in the next verse (Exodus 3:15), not derived from ehyeh asher ehyeh; Aquinas's view (ST I q.13 a.11) attributed to him rather than spoken as "the deepest thing we can say"; word line attributed.
Douay-Rheims Exodus 3:14 ('God said to Moses: I AM WHO AM. He said: Thus shalt thou say to the children of Israel: HE WHO IS, hath sent me to you.') and John 8:58 given from memory; confirm.
Hebrew pointing and pronunciation of ehyeh asher ehyeh; confirm.
'Every other god in the ancient world had a name that could be used, invoked, even bargained with' is a generalization; a Keeper may want it softened.
The 2008 Congregation for Divine Worship directive on not pronouncing the divine name in the liturgy is described in howItsDone; confirm wording.
